children: Gold's near-term outlook is clouded by expectations of higher U.S. interest rates, but central-bank buying is set to drive prices back above $4,600 a troy ounce by the end of next year, Goldman Sachs said in its latest report.

The bank expects gold to reach $4,650 a troy ounce by the end of 2027, about 13% above its October average, as central-bank purchases--particularly by emerging-market countries seeking to diversify their reserves--emerge as the main force supporting prices.
In midmorning European trading on Tuesday, gold futures in New York traded 0.4% higher at $3,869 an ounce, down more than 7% on the month.

Central-bank purchases are forecast to average 60 tons a month through 2028, more than three times the average seen before 2022. Emerging-market central banks have stepped up gold buying since the freezing of Russian reserves, reflecting efforts to reduce reliance on Western currencies and diversify their holdings, analysts at Goldman said.

The near-term outlook remains challenging. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates again in December and March, making gold less attractive to investors because it pays no interest, according to the bank's estimates. Higher borrowing costs could also prompt investors to pull money from gold-backed exchange-traded funds, putting pressure on prices.

But the picture could improve once the Fed starts cutting rates. Goldman expects four rate cuts between November 2027 and September 2028, reviving demand from Western investors and helping push gold to $5,600 an ounce by the end of 2028.
